title: Fetch the tax tables once, and let checkouts read them without queueing

blocks.text: Checkout computes VAT from tables that the tax service publishes. Fetching them takes seconds and the tax service bills every call, so the shop fetches them the first time a checkout needs them and keeps them. At peak, a few hundred thousand checkouts a second ask for the tables, from many threads. Last quarter's version fetched the tables twice during the morning rush, and the version before it made every checkout wait in line for the tables.

Finish `src/main/java/practice/TaxTables.java`: the body of `rates()`, and the declaration of the `rates` field it keeps the tables in (there is a `TODO` on each). Use the `lock` field the class already has.

items: the tax service is called on the first call to `rates()` and never again, even when two checkouts make the first call at the same moment;
once the tables are fetched, `rates()` returns them without waiting, even while some other thread holds the lock;
a checkout on any thread that gets the tables gets them as the tax service built them.

blocks.text: About ten lines in total. Some of the tests hold the tax service or the lock on one thread and call `rates()` on another; one of them also reads how the `rates` field is declared.

cases.says: nothing is fetched until the first call; later calls return the same tables without fetching again
a second caller that arrives while the first fetch is running waits for it and gets its tables, and the tax service is called once
once the tables are fetched, a call returns them even while another thread holds the lock
the field that calls read without the lock is volatile, so a caller that sees the reference sees the finished tables

origin.section: Double-Checked Locking Reads Without the Lock, So Its Field Must Be volatile

concepts: Double-checked locking's first check reads without the lock, so without a volatile field a caller can get a reference to an object whose constructor's writes it doesn't see.
The check under the lock is what stops a second caller that also found the field empty from creating the object again.
